title: Participatory Research and Practice Innovation
reference_framework: IFSW ethical principles; course-specific inquiry design examples require research-methods review

modules.title: Practice questions and meaningful participation
modules.outcome: Frame an answerable practice question and plan meaningful, voluntary participation.

teaching_points.text: An answerable practice question identifies a specific issue, population or setting and a feasible inquiry; it should not assume its conclusion.
Meaningful participation includes influence over relevant questions and interpretation, with roles and limits agreed in advance.
Separate participation choices from service eligibility; make refusal possible without threatening support, and manage power differences.
Researchers should reflect on how their role and assumptions influence questions, recruitment and interpretation; reflection does not eliminate bias.
Agree co-researcher roles, support, compensation arrangements where applicable, access and confidentiality expectations before tasks begin.

modules.title: Ethical inquiry and interpretation
modules.outcome: Collect proportionate information and interpret findings without overstating what the inquiry can show.

teaching_points.text: Choose the minimum information needed for the question and keep recruitment contacts separate from responses where feasible.
Small groups can be identifiable through combinations of details even when names are removed; review quotations and context before sharing.
Recruitment methods shape whose experiences are represented; describe missing perspectives and avoid generalising beyond the sample.
Conflicting findings should be explored and reported transparently, not removed merely to make a simple story.
A before-and-after change alone does not establish that a pilot caused the result; consider other explanations and design limits.

modules.title: Responsible innovation and learning
modules.outcome: Plan a bounded, reviewable service pilot with safeguards and a useful feedback loop.

teaching_points.text: Before a pilot, define the scope, participants, risks, responsible people and criteria for continuing, changing or stopping.
A pilot label does not exempt a project from research-ethics or governance review; obtain the relevant determination before data collection.
Stop or pause criteria should lead to timely review when harms or barriers emerge; completing the pilot schedule is not the only priority.
Record adaptations and their timing so later readers know which version participants experienced.
Return understandable findings to participants, explain limits and decisions, and offer a feasible way to respond.

questions.question: Which question is best suited to a small inquiry about missed appointments at one service?

options.text: What explains every missed appointment in the world?
Why are all people who miss appointments irresponsible?
What barriers do participating service users describe when attending appointments at this service?
How can this team prove its service is perfect?

questions.rationale: The bounded question can be explored without presuming blame or claiming universal reach.

questions.question: Residents are invited only to approve a finished research report. What would give them more meaningful influence in the next inquiry?

options.text: Replace discussion with a photograph for the report
Agree involvement in framing questions and interpreting findings before collection starts
Invite only residents who already agree with the conclusions
Ask for more signatures on the final cover page

questions.rationale: Early and substantive roles can influence the inquiry. End-stage endorsement alone provides limited participation.

questions.question: A service user thinks declining an interview will jeopardise their support. What should the team address before recruitment continues?

options.text: Clarify and protect voluntary choice and separate recruitment from service decisions
Ask the caseworker to insist on participation
Use the fear to obtain more responses
Treat receipt of support as automatic research consent

questions.rationale: The perceived dependency undermines free choice. The recruitment process must address the power relationship.

questions.question: A worker researching their own service believes its new process must be effective. What should they do with that assumption?

options.text: Rewrite questions so every answer supports the process
Treat their job role as proof of objectivity
Record it and seek methods and perspectives that can challenge it
Exclude any account that contradicts it

questions.rationale: Making the assumption visible and allowing challenge helps manage its influence; it does not guarantee neutrality.

questions.question: A resident co-researcher is asked to interview neighbours without training or a role agreement. What should happen first?

options.text: Require them to disclose neighbours' stories at a public meeting
Assume living locally replaces preparation
Agree the role and boundaries, provide appropriate support and review privacy risks
Give them unrestricted access to all case files

questions.rationale: Local experience is valuable but does not replace clear responsibilities, preparation and information safeguards.

questions.question: A satisfaction inquiry proposes collecting identity numbers although its question concerns appointment times. What should the team reconsider?

options.text: Whether irrelevant identifiers guarantee truthful answers
Whether identifiers are necessary and whether less identifying information can answer the question
Whether more identifiers would make the report look rigorous
Whether responses can be posted with full identities

questions.rationale: Identity numbers do not inherently help answer a scheduling question and add avoidable information risk.

questions.question: A report removes names but describes the only wheelchair user in a small village by job and household details. What is the main risk?

options.text: The person may still be identifiable from the combined description
The description cannot be sensitive because it is written in prose
The report becomes automatically anonymous once names are removed
Confidentiality matters only for numeric data

questions.rationale: Indirect details can identify someone in context. Name removal alone is not a sufficient privacy check.

questions.question: An online survey reaches only residents who follow the service's social-media page. What should the report acknowledge?

options.text: People outside that channel may have different experiences that the survey did not capture
Every resident had an equal chance to respond
The findings prove the views of all non-users
The response count removes any recruitment limitation

questions.rationale: Channel-based recruitment can miss important groups regardless of the total response count.

questions.question: Interviews praise a service, but appointment records show persistent drop-out. What is the best next step?

options.text: Discard the interviews because numbers always override experience
Explore the difference in what each source measures and report relevant limitations
Average the statements into an unsupported single score
Delete the records because interviews are more positive

questions.rationale: Different sources can describe different experiences or populations. The discrepancy may be informative.

questions.question: Attendance rises after a reminder pilot during the same month transport becomes free. What can the team reasonably conclude?

options.text: Attendance improved, but the pilot's separate contribution is uncertain
Free transport could not have any influence
The reminder pilot alone caused the entire increase
A before-and-after comparison proves causation in every case

questions.rationale: Concurrent changes create alternative explanations. The observed improvement is not enough to isolate the reminder's effect.

questions.question: A team wants to try a new intake process. Which preparation best supports a responsible pilot?

options.text: Define success only after results are known
Remove the current route before checking alternatives
Roll it out everywhere without a review date
Set a limited scope, safeguards, decision criteria and review responsibilities

questions.rationale: A bounded plan supports a defensible decision and protects participants while uncertainty remains.

questions.question: A team says ethics review cannot apply because it calls its project 'service innovation'. What should it do?

options.text: Begin collecting sensitive data while avoiding any record
Tell participants that pilots have no privacy requirements
Assume the label settles the issue
Ask the relevant governance or ethics body to determine the applicable requirements

questions.rationale: The activity and its risks, not just its label, determine which review requirements apply.

questions.question: A new booking pilot repeatedly leaves participants unable to access urgent appointments. What is the best response?

options.text: Wait until the scheduled final report before raising the issue
Continue unchanged to obtain a larger sample
Remove those participants from the findings
Use the agreed safety and escalation route and review whether to pause or change the pilot

questions.rationale: Emerging access risks need timely action. More observations do not justify ignoring the problem.

questions.question: Halfway through a pilot, staff change the reminder script. What record is needed for interpretation?

options.text: Only the best outcome from either version
A combined result that hides the change
What changed, why, when and which participants experienced each version
Only the original script because that was approved first

questions.rationale: Version and timing information help explain results and prevent attributing every outcome to a single unchanged intervention.

questions.question: An inquiry ends with a technical report sent only to funders. What would improve accountability to participants?

options.text: Assume participants do not want to know the outcome
Share an accessible summary, explain decisions and limitations, and provide a feedback route
Publish identifiable raw interviews to show transparency
Promise every suggestion will be adopted

questions.rationale: An accessible feedback loop respects participation without promising agreement or exposing private data.
